He is doubtful and perplexed regarding the Teacher, does not resolve upon him, and does not have faith in him; he is doubtful and perplexed regarding the Dhamma, does not resolve upon it, and does not have faith in it;
he is doubtful and perplexed regarding the Saṅgha, does not resolve upon it, and does not have faith in it;
he is doubtful and perplexed regarding the training, does not resolve upon it, and does not have faith in it; and he is angry toward his fellow celibates.
One becomes displeased, with a mind struck down and born of barrenness—
these are the five mental barrennesses.
In this regard, what are the five mental bondages?
He is not free from lust for sensual pleasures; he has not abandoned desire, not abandoned affection, not abandoned thirst, not abandoned fever, and not abandoned craving for them.
He is not free from lust for the body… he is not free from lust for forms…
Having eaten as much as he desires until his belly is full, he dwells devoted to the pleasure of sleep, the pleasure of reclining, and the pleasure of drowsiness;
and he leads the holy life aspiring for some order of gods, thinking, “By this virtue, or vow, or austerity, or holy life, I shall become a god or one of the higher gods.
These are the five mental bondages.
In this context, what are the five hindrances?
The hindrance of sensual desire, the hindrance of ill will, the hindrance of sloth and torpor, the hindrance of restlessness and remorse,
and the hindrance of doubt— these are the five hindrances.
In this regard, what are the five actions that have immediate retribution?
One has deprived one’s mother of life; one has deprived one’s father of life; one has deprived an Arhat of life; with a malicious mind, one has shed the blood of a Tathāgata;
one has caused a schism in the Saṅgha—these are the five actions that have immediate retribution.
In this regard, what are the five views? Some assert:
"The self exists as percipient and healthy after death"; some assert: "The self exists as non-percipient and healthy after death";
[some assert]: "The self exists as neither percipient nor non-percipient and healthy after death."
In this regard, some proclaim [one of these views]: they describe the annihilation, destruction, and non-existence of an existing being;
or some proclaim Nibbāna in the present life—these are the five views.
In this context, what are the five enmities?
Killing living beings, taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, false speech, and the use of fermented and distilled liquors that cause negligence—
these are the five enmities.
In this regard, what are the five calamities?
The calamity of relatives, the calamity of wealth, the calamity of disease, the calamity of moral conduct, and the calamity of views—
these are the five calamities.
In this regard, what are the five disadvantages of impatience?

One is disliked and displeasing to many people; one has much enmity and much fault; one dies confused; and with the breakup of the body, after death, one is reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, or hell.
These are the five disadvantages of impatience.
In this regard, what are the five fears?
Fear for one’s livelihood, fear of ill repute, fear of timidity before an assembly, fear of death, and fear of a bad rebirth—
these are the five fears.
In this regard, what are the five doctrines of Nibbāna in the present life?
Here, a certain ascetic or brahmin holds such a doctrine and such a view:
"Sirs, when this self is endowed with and possessed of the five cords of sensual pleasure and enjoys them, to that extent, sirs, this self has attained the supreme Nibbāna in the present life."
In this way, some proclaim the supreme Nibbāna in this very life for an existing being.
Another says to him:
"Sir, there is indeed this self of which you speak; I do not say that it does not exist."
But, sir, this self does not thereby attain supreme Nibbāna in the present life. And why is that?
Because sensual pleasures, sir, are impermanent, suffering, and subject to change.
“From their change and alteration, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair arise.
But when, sir, this self, secluded from sensual pleasures... enters and dwells in the first jhāna, to that extent, sir, this self has attained the supreme Nibbāna in the present life.
In this way, some describe the supreme Nibbāna in the present life for an existing being.
Another said this to him:
“Sir, there indeed is that self of which you speak.
I do not say that it does not exist.”
But, sir, this self does not yet attain supreme Nibbāna in the present life to that extent.
And why is that? Because whatever is thought and deliberated upon therein, by that very fact it is declared to be gross.

"But when, sir, with the subsiding of applied and sustained thought, this self enters and dwells in the second jhāna... it is at this point, sir, that this self has attained the supreme Nibbāna in the present life.
Thus some describe the supreme Nibbāna in the present life for an existing being.
To this, another says:
“Indeed, sir, there is this self of which you speak.
I do not say that it does not exist.
Yet, sir, this self does not thereby attain supreme Nibbāna in this very life.”
And why is that? Because whatever state of rapture there is, whatever elation of the mind, by that this [self] is declared to be gross.
But when, sir, through the fading away of rapture... [and so on].
"Having attained and dwelled in the third jhāna, to this extent, sir, this self has attained the supreme Nibbāna in this very life.
In this way, some describe the supreme Nibbāna in this very life for an existing being.
To them, another says this:
“Sir, there is indeed this self of which you speak.
I do not say that it does not exist.
However, sir, this self has not yet attained the supreme Nibbāna in this very life to such an extent.”
"And for what reason?
Because whatever mental attention there is toward pleasure and rapture therein, by that it is declared to be gross.
But when, sir, this self, through the abandoning of pleasure... enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna, to that extent, sir, this self has attained the supreme Nibbāna in this very life."
In this way, some proclaim the supreme Nibbāna in this very life for an existing being.
These are the five doctrines of Nibbāna in this very life.
This concludes the group of five.
6. Exposition of the Six.
Therein, what are the six roots of dispute?
Anger, hypocrisy, envy, deceitfulness, evil desire, and adherence to one's own views.
These are the six roots of dispute.
In this regard, what are the six kinds of desire-and-lust?
They are the desire-and-lust for things associated with the household life.
Lust for agreeable forms, infatuation with agreeable forms, the infatuation of the mind with agreeable forms;
[and so on] for agreeable sounds … for agreeable odors … for agreeable tastes … [and so on].
In regard to pleasant tactile objects …pe… in regard to pleasant mental phenomena,
there is lust based on the household life, infatuation, and the infatuation of the mind—
these are the six types of desire-lust.
In this context, what are the six bases of opposition?

Mental irritation, resentment, ferocity, abruptness, and displeasure of mind toward disagreeable forms; [the same] toward disagreeable sounds …pe… toward disagreeable odors …pe… [toward disagreeable tastes, tangible objects, and mental phenomena].
In unpleasant tastes …pe… in unpleasant tangible objects …pe… in unpleasant mental phenomena,
there is resentment, hostility, irritability, abruptness, and displeasure of mind.
These are the six bases of conflict.
In this regard, what are the six groups of craving?
Craving for forms, craving for sounds, craving for odors, craving for tastes, craving for tangibles, and craving for mental phenomena.
These are the six groups of craving.
In this context, what are the six kinds of disrespect?
One dwells with disrespect and lack of deference toward the Teacher; one dwells with disrespect and lack of deference toward the Dharma; one dwells with disrespect [toward the Saṅgha]...
He dwells without deference; he dwells disrespectful and undeferential toward the training, toward heedfulness, and toward hospitality—
these are the six kinds of disrespect.
In this regard, what are the six factors of decline?
Delight in work, delight in talk, delight in sleep, delight in company, delight in socializing, and delight in conceptual proliferation—
these are the six factors of decline.
In this regard, what are the other six factors of decline?
Delight in work, delight in talk, delight in sleep, delight in company, being difficult to correct, and having evil friends—
these are the six factors of decline.
In this context, what are the six explorations of mental joy (*somanassūpavicāra*)?
Having seen a form with the eye, one explores a form that is a basis for joy; having heard a sound with the ear...
[and so on] ...having smelled an odor with the nose... [and so on].
Having tasted a flavor with the tongue … having touched a tangible object with the body … having cognized a mental phenomenon with the mind,
one dwells upon a mental phenomenon that is a basis for joy.
These are the six explorations of mental joy.
In this context, what are the six explorations of mental grief?
Having seen a form with the eye, one explores a form that is a basis for mental grief; having heard a sound with the ear... [and so on].
Having smelled an odor with the nose …pe… having tasted a flavor with the tongue …pe… having touched a tangible object with the body …pe…
Having cognized a mental phenomenon with the mind, one dwells upon a phenomenon that is a basis for displeasure—
these are the six modes of dwelling in displeasure.
In this context, what are the six modes of dwelling in equanimity?
Having seen a form with the eye, one explores a form that is a basis for equanimity;
having heard a sound with the ear …pe… having smelled an odor with the nose …pe… having tasted a flavor with the tongue …pe…
Having touched a tangible object with the body …pe… having cognized a mental phenomenon with the mind, one explores a phenomenon that is a basis for equanimity—
these are the six explorations of equanimity.
In this context, what are the six kinds of worldly joy?

It is the mental state of satisfaction, the mental state of pleasure, born of mental contact, the feeling of satisfaction and pleasure born of mental contact—the pleasant and joyful sensation born of mental contact—with respect to agreeable forms; [likewise] with respect to agreeable sounds...
[and so on] ...with respect to agreeable odors... [and so on].
In regard to agreeable tastes …pe… agreeable tangibles …pe… agreeable mental phenomena,
there is mental pleasure, mental happiness, a pleasant and happy feeling born of mental contact, and a pleasant and happy sensation born of mental contact.
These are the six kinds of worldly joy.
In this context, what are the six kinds of worldly displeasure?

Regarding unpleasant forms, there is mental unease, mental pain, mental suffering born of contact with the mind; an unpleasant, painful feeling born of contact with the mind, an unpleasant and painful sensation born of contact with the mind. [The same applies to] unpleasant sounds... [and so on].
...regarding unpleasant odors ...pe...
regarding unpleasant tastes ...pe...
regarding unpleasant tactile objects ...pe...
In regard to disagreeable phenomena, there is mental unease, mental suffering, a disagreeable painful experience born of mind-contact, and a disagreeable painful feeling born of mind-contact—
these are the six types of household-based displeasure (*domanassa*).
In this context, what are the six types of household-based equanimity (*upekkhā*)?

In regard to forms that are objects of equanimity, there is mental feeling born of contact with the mind, neither pleasant nor unpleasant, which is neither painful nor pleasant; this is mental feeling born of contact with the mind that is neither painful nor pleasant.
[The same applies] to sounds that are objects of equanimity … to odors that are objects of equanimity … to tastes that are objects of equanimity … [and so forth].
In regard to tangible objects that are a basis for equanimity …pe… in regard to mental phenomena that are a basis for equanimity,
there is a mental feeling born of mental contact that is neither pleasant nor unpleasant, a feeling born of mental contact that is neither painful nor pleasant;
these are the six kinds of worldly equanimity.
In this context, what are the six views?
Either the view arises in him, firmly and truly, that "there is a self for me," or the view arises in him, firmly and truly, that "there is no self for me."
Or else, the view arises in him as something true and firm: “I perceive self by means of self”;
or the view arises in him as something true and firm: “I perceive not-self by means of self”;
or the view arises in him as something true and firm: “I perceive self by means of not-self.”
Or else, he has such a view as this: “This self of mine is one that speaks and feels, which for a long time experiences here and there the result of wholesome and unwholesome kamma.

It was not born, it did not come to be; it will not be born, it will not come to be. It is permanent, stable, eternal, and not subject to change. Or else, such a view arises in him as something true and established.
These are the six views.
The Hexad.
7. Exposition of the Heptad.
Therein, what are the seven underlying tendencies?

The underlying tendency to sensual lust, the underlying tendency to aversion, the underlying tendency to conceit, the underlying tendency to views, the underlying tendency to doubt, the underlying tendency to lust for existence, and the underlying tendency to ignorance— these are the seven underlying tendencies.
In this context, what are the seven fetters?
The fetter of sensual lust, the fetter of aversion, the fetter of conceit, the fetter of views, the fetter of doubt, the fetter of lust for existence, and the fetter of ignorance—
these are the seven fetters. In this context, what are the seven obsessions?

The obsession of sensual lust, the obsession of aversion, the obsession of conceit, the obsession of views, the obsession of doubt, the obsession of lust for existence, and the obsession of ignorance—
these are the seven obsessions. In this context,
what are the seven things that are not the True Dhamma?
One is faithless, shameless, reckless, of little learning, lazy, muddle-minded, and unwise—
these are the seven unwholesome qualities.
In this context, what are the seven types of misconduct?
Taking life, taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, false speech, malicious speech, harsh speech, and idle chatter—
these are the seven types of misconduct.
In this context, what are the seven kinds of conceit?
Conceit, over-conceit, conceit beyond conceit, inferiority-conceit, superiority-conceit, the conceit "I am," and false conceit—
these are the seven types of conceit.
In this context, what are the seven views?
In this case, some ascetic or brahmin holds such a doctrine and such a view:

"Sirs, when this self—which possesses form, is composed of the four great elements, and is born of mother and father—is cut off and destroyed at the breaking up of the body and does not exist after death, to that extent, sirs, this self is completely annihilated.
In this way, some proclaim the annihilation, destruction, and non-existence of an existing being.
Then another said this:
"Sir, there indeed is that self of which you speak.
I do not say that it does not exist."
But, sir, this self is not completely annihilated by that much.
There is, sir, another self, divine, material, belonging to the sense-sphere, and subsisting on solid food;
you do not know it, nor do you see it.
"I know that self; I see it.
That self, sir, is annihilated and destroyed with the breakup of the body and does not exist after death. To this extent, sir, this self is completely annihilated.
In this way, some proclaim the annihilation, destruction, and non-existence of a being.
Another said this to him:
"Sir, there certainly is such a self as you speak of.
I do not say that it does not exist."
"But, sir, this self is not completely annihilated by that much.
There is, sir, another self— divine, material, mind-made, complete in all its limbs and parts, with no faculties lacking—
that you neither know nor see."
"I know that, I see that.
For that self, sir, when at the breaking up of the body is cut off, destroyed, and does not exist after death—to this extent, sir, this self is completely annihilated.
In this way, some proclaim the annihilation, destruction, and non-existence of an existing being.
Another said this to him:
"Sir, there indeed is that self of which you speak.
I do not say that it does not exist."
But, sir, this self is not completely annihilated by that much.

There is, sir, another self which, with the complete surmounting of perceptions of form, with the disappearance of perceptions of sensory impact, and with non-attention to perceptions of diversity, [perceiving] "space is infinite," has reached the base of infinite space.
You do not know it, you do not see it.
"I know that, I see that.
For that self, sir, when at the breaking up of the body is cut off, destroyed, and does not exist after death—to this extent, sir, this self is completely annihilated.
In this way, some proclaim the annihilation, destruction, and non-existence of an existing being.
Another said this to him:
"Sir, there certainly is such a self as you speak of.
I do not say that it does not exist."
"But, sir, this self is not completely annihilated by that much.
There is, sir, another self that, having entirely transcended the base of infinite space, enters upon the base of infinite consciousness, thinking 'consciousness is infinite.
You do not know it, you do not see it."
"I know that, I see that.
For that self, sir, when at the breaking up of the body is cut off, perishes, and does not exist after death—to this extent, sir, this self is completely annihilated.
In this way, some proclaim the annihilation, destruction, and non-existence of an existing being.
Another said this to him:
“Sir, there indeed is that self of which you speak.
I do not say that it does not exist.”
But, sir, this self is not completely annihilated by that much.
There is, sir, another self which, having completely transcended the base of infinite consciousness, enters upon the base of nothingness, thinking "there is nothing.
You do not know it, you do not see it.
“I know that self; I see it.
That self, sir, is annihilated and destroyed with the breakup of the body and does not exist after death. To this extent, sir, this self is completely annihilated.
In this way, some proclaim the annihilation, destruction, and non-existence of an existing being.
Another said this to him:
"There indeed is that self of which you speak.
I do not say, 'It does not exist.'"
But, sir, this self is not completely annihilated by that much.
There is, sir, another self that, having entirely transcended the base of nothingness, has reached the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;
you do not know it, nor do you see it.
“I know that, I see that.
For that self, sir, when at the breaking up of the body is cut off, perishes, and does not exist after death—to this extent, sir, this self is completely annihilated.
In this way, some proclaim the annihilation, destruction, and non-existence of an existing being.
These are the seven views.
[End of] the Section on the Sevens.
8. Exposition of the Eights.
In this context, what are the eight bases of defilement?
Greed, hatred, delusion, conceit, wrong view, doubt, sloth, and restlessness—
these are the eight bases of defilement.
In this regard, what are the eight bases of laziness?
Here, a task must be done by a bhikkhu.
It occurs to him:
“I must perform some work. While performing that work, my body will become weary.
Come now, I shall lie down.”
Thus he lies down; he does not arouse energy for the attainment of the unattained, for the reaching of the unreached, for the realization of the unrealized.
This is the first ground of laziness.
Furthermore, a deed has been done by the bhikkhu.
It occurs to him:
"I have indeed performed an action;
while performing that action, my body has become weary."
"Come now, I shall lie down. He lies down;
he does not arouse energy for the attainment of the unattained, for the reaching of the unreached, for the realization of the unrealized.
This is the second ground of laziness.
Furthermore, there comes a time when a bhikkhu must travel along a road.
It occurs to him:
"I must travel along a road."
"Moreover, my body will grow weary from walking along the road.
Come now, I shall lie down. He lies down;
he does not arouse energy for the attainment of the unattained, for the reaching of the unreached, for the realization of the unrealized.
This is the third ground for laziness.
Furthermore, a bhikkhu has traveled along a road,
and this thought occurs to him:
“I have indeed traveled along the road.
As I was traveling along the road, my body is weary.
Come now, I shall lie down.”
Thus he lies down; he does not arouse energy for the attainment of the unattained, for the reaching of the unreached, for the realization of the unrealized.
This is the fourth ground of laziness.
Furthermore, a bhikkhu, while wandering for alms in a village or town, does not obtain sufficient or complete food, whether coarse or refined, to satisfy his needs.
It occurs to him:
"While wandering for alms in a village or town, I did not obtain as much coarse or refined food as I required for full satisfaction.
Consequently, my body is weary and unfit for work."
"Come now, I shall lie down. He lies down;
he does not arouse energy for the attainment of the unattained, for the reaching of the unreached, for the realization of the unrealized.
This is the fifth ground of laziness.
Furthermore, when a bhikkhu, while wandering for alms in a village or town, obtains as much food as he requires, whether coarse or refined, it occurs to him:
"While wandering for alms in a village or town, I have obtained as much food as I required, whether coarse or refined."
“My body is weary and unfit for work, as if covered with a layer of fat.
Come now, I shall lie down. He lies down;
he does not arouse energy for the attainment of the unattained, for the reaching of the unreached, or for the realization of the unrealized.
This is the sixth ground for laziness.
Furthermore, a slight illness arises in a bhikkhu.
It occurs to him:
“This slight ailment has arisen in me.
It is appropriate for me to lie down.
Come now, I shall lie down.”
Thus he lies down; he does not arouse energy for the attainment of the unattained, for the reaching of the unreached, for the realization of the unrealized.
This is the seventh ground of laziness.
Furthermore, a bhikkhu has recently recovered from an illness and has not long been free from it.
It occurs to him:
"I have indeed recovered from illness; it has not been long since I arose from that sickness.
My body is weak and unfit for work."
"Come now, I shall lie down. He lies down;
he does not arouse energy for the attainment of the unattained, for the reaching of the unreached, for the realization of the unrealized.
This is the eighth ground of laziness.
These are the eight bases of laziness.
In that regard, what is the resistance of the mind toward the eight worldly conditions?
Attachment to gain and aversion to loss; attachment to fame and aversion to disrepute; attachment to praise and aversion to blame; attachment to pleasure and aversion to pain.
The repulsion of the mind toward these eight worldly conditions.
In this context, what are the eight ignoble modes of speech?

Claiming to have seen what was not seen; claiming to have heard what was not heard; claiming to have sensed what was not sensed; claiming to have cognized what was not cognized; claiming not to have seen what was seen; claiming not to have heard what was heard; claiming not to have sensed what was sensed; and claiming not to have cognized what was cognized.
These are the eight ignoble modes of speech.
In that regard, what are the eight wrong states?
Wrong view, wrong intention, wrong speech, wrong action, wrong livelihood, wrong effort, wrong mindfulness, and wrong concentration.
These are the eight wrong states.
In that regard, what are the eight faults of a person?
Here, monks reprove a monk for an offense.
Thus, when a bhikkhu is being accused of an offense by other bhikkhus, he evades it through sheer forgetfulness, saying, "I do not remember, I do not remember.
This is the first fault of a person.
Furthermore, bhikkhus accuse a bhikkhu of an offense.
Thus, when that bhikkhu is being charged with an offense by the bhikkhus, he retorts against the accuser himself:
"What is the use of what you, a fool and incompetent, have to say?
Do you really think that you, too, should be spoken to by me?"
This is the second fault of a person.
Furthermore, monks reprove a monk for an offense.
While being reproved by the monks for that offense, that monk counters the reprover with a charge of his own.
“You too have fallen into such-and-such an offense.
You, therefore, should first make amends.
This is the third fault of a person.
Furthermore, monks, when monks reprove a monk for an offense, that monk,
being reproved by the monks for an offense, evades the issue with irrelevant talk, diverts the conversation to external matters, and displays anger, hatred, and resentment.
This is the fourth fault of a person.
Furthermore, monks accuse a monk of an offense.
While being accused of an offense by the monks, that monk speaks with gesticulating arms in the midst of the Saṅgha.
This is the fifth fault of a man.
Furthermore, monks accuse a monk of an offense.
While being accused by the monks of an offense, that monk, thinking, "I have neither committed an offense, nor have I not committed one," harasses the Saṅgha by remaining silent.
This is the sixth fault of a person.
Furthermore, monks, they reprove a monk for an offense.
While being reproved by the monks for that offense, that monk, disregarding the Saṅgha and disregarding the reprover, departs wherever he wishes while still possessed of the offense.
This is the seventh fault of a person.
Furthermore, monks exhort a monk regarding an offense.
Being exhorted by the monks regarding that offense, that monk says this:
"Why, venerable sirs, are you so excessively preoccupied with me?"
"Now, having renounced the training, I shall return to the lower life.
Having renounced the training and returned to the lower life, he said:
"Now, venerable sirs, you may be satisfied."
This is the eighth fault of a person.
These are the eight faults of a person.
In this regard, what are the eight views of non-percipient beings?
“The self is material and healthy after death”—
thus they describe it as being non-percipient;
[or] the self is immaterial … [and so on].
“Both possessing form and formless …pe… neither possessing form nor formless …pe… ‘The self is finite and free from disease after death’”— thus [he asserts].
They describe him as "non-percipient":
"The self is infinite and healthy after death"—
thus they describe him as non-percipient.
“The self is both finite and infinite, and is healthy after death”—
thus they describe it as non-percipient.
“The self is neither finite nor infinite, and is healthy after death”— thus [they describe it].
“They describe him as ‘non-percipient.
These are the eight doctrines of non-perception.
In this context, what are the eight doctrines of neither-perception-nor-non-perception?”
“The self is material and healthy after death”—
thus they describe it as neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient;
“the self is immaterial and healthy after death”— thus they describe it.
They describe it as "neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient";
they describe it thus: "The self is both material and immaterial, healthy after death"—they describe it as "neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient."
‘The self is neither material nor immaterial and is unimpaired after death’—
they describe it as ‘neither percipient nor non-percipient’;
‘the self is finite and is unimpaired after death’— they describe it thus.
They describe him as "neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient";
they describe him thus: "The self is infinite and healthy after death, neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient."
“The self is both finite and infinite, and is unimpaired after death”—
thus they describe it as being neither percipient nor non-percipient.
“The self is neither finite nor infinite, and is unimpaired after death”— thus [they describe it].
They describe him as "neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient. These are the eight views concerning neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
This concludes the section of eight.
9. The Exposition of the Ninefold Set.
Therein, what are the nine grounds for resentment?
“He has done me harm,” thus resentment arises;
“‘He has done me harm’—thus resentment arises;
‘He will do me harm’—thus resentment arises;
‘He has done harm to one who is dear and pleasing to me’ … [and so on] …”
“He has acted for my harm … he will act for my harm,” thus resentment arises;
“He has acted for the benefit of one who is disagreeable and unpleasant to me …” [and so on].
“He is acting for my benefit,” … “he will act for my benefit”— thus resentment arises.
These are the nine grounds for resentment.
In this regard, what are the nine stains of a person?
Anger, hypocrisy, envy, avarice, deceit, craftiness, false speech, evil desire, and wrong view—
these are the nine stains of a person.
In this context, what are the nine kinds of conceit?
The conceit, "I am superior to one who is superior"; the conceit, "I am equal to one who is superior"; the conceit, "I am inferior to one who is superior";
the conceit, "I am superior to one who is equal"; the conceit, "I am equal to one who is equal"; the conceit, "I am... [inferior to one who is equal]".
The conceit, "I am inferior"; the conceit, "I am superior to one who is inferior"; the conceit, "I am equal to one who is inferior";
the conceit, "I am inferior to one who is inferior"—these are the nine kinds of conceit.
In this context, what are the nine states rooted in craving?
Dependent on craving comes seeking; dependent on seeking comes gain; dependent on gain comes decision-making;
dependent on decision-making comes desire and lust; dependent on desire and lust comes attachment; dependent on attachment...
Possession; dependent on possession, stinginess; dependent on stinginess, guarding;
and because of guarding, there arise many evil unwholesome states—taking up sticks and weapons, quarrels, strife, disputes, contention, slander, and false speech.
These are the nine states rooted in craving.
In this regard, what are the nine perturbations?
“I am”—this is a perturbation; “I am this”—this is a perturbation; “I am such a one”—this is a perturbation; “I shall be”—this is a perturbation;
“I shall be possessed of form”—this is a perturbation; “I shall be formless”—this is a perturbation; “I shall be percipient”...
“I shall exist” is a fluctuation; “I shall be non-percipient” is a fluctuation; “I shall be neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient” is a fluctuation—these are the nine fluctuations.
In this context, what are the nine conceits? …pe…
What are the nine tremblings …pe… the nine proliferations …pe… the nine conditioned phenomena?
“I am” is conditioned; “I am this” is conditioned; “This I am” is conditioned; “I shall be” is conditioned;
“I shall be possessed of form” is conditioned; “I shall be formless” is conditioned;
“I shall be percipient” is conditioned; “I shall be non-percipient” is conditioned.
“I shall be neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient”—this is conditioned.
These are the nine conditioned things. –9.
The Group of Nine.
10. Exposition of the Ten [Defilements] (Dasakaniddesa).
Therein, what are the ten bases of defilement?
Greed, hatred, delusion, conceit, wrong view, doubt, sloth, restlessness, lack of moral shame, and lack of moral dread.
These are the ten bases of defilement. In that regard, what are the ten bases of resentment?

Resentment arises thinking, "He has done me harm"; resentment arises thinking, "He is doing me harm"; resentment arises thinking, "He will do me harm"; resentment arises thinking, "He has done harm to one who is dear and pleasing to me" ... [and so on].
“...he has acted for my harm...

he will act for my harm,” thus resentment arises; “...he has acted for the benefit of one who is disagreeable and unpleasant to me... he is acting for their benefit... he will act for their benefit,” thus resentment arises.
“He will pursue my welfare”—thus resentment arises; or else resentment arises where there is no ground for it.
These are the ten grounds for resentment.
In this regard, what are the ten unwholesome courses of action?
Killing living beings, taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, false speech, malicious speech, harsh speech, idle chatter, covetousness, ill will, and wrong view—
these are the ten courses of unwholesome action.
In this context, what are the ten fetters?
The fetter of sensual lust, the fetter of aversion, the fetter of conceit, the fetter of views, the fetter of doubt,
the fetter of adherence to rules and observances, the fetter of lust for existence, the fetter of envy, the fetter of avarice,
and the fetter of ignorance— these are the ten fetters.
In this context, what are the ten wrong states?
Wrong view, wrong intention, wrong speech, wrong action, wrong livelihood, wrong effort, wrong mindfulness, wrong concentration, wrong knowledge,
and wrong liberation— these are the ten wrong states.
In this regard, what is wrong view with ten bases? It is:
"There is no giving, there is no sacrifice, there is no offering; there is no fruit or result of deeds well done or ill done;
there is no this world, there is no other world; there is no mother, there is no father; there are no beings..."
“Beings are spontaneously born; there are no recluses or brahmins in the world who have attained the right path and practiced rightly, who,
having realized this world and the other world for themselves through direct knowledge, make them known”—
this is the tenfold wrong view.
In this context, what is the view of grasping at extremes consisting of ten bases?
It is: "The world is eternal," or "the world is non-eternal"; "the world is finite," or "the world is infinite";
"the soul and the body are the same," or "the soul and the body are different"; or "a Tathāgata exists after death."

Or, "The Tathāgata exists after death," or "The Tathāgata does not exist after death," or "The Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death," or "The Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death"—
this is the tenfold view that clings to extremes.
The Decad.
11. Exposition of the Wanderings of Craving.
Therein, what are the eighteen wanderings of craving based on the internal?
"I am" occurs; "I am thus" occurs; "I am like this" occurs; "I am otherwise" occurs; "I shall be" occurs;
"I shall be thus" occurs; "I shall be like this" occurs; "I shall be otherwise" occurs;
"I might be" occurs; "I might be thus" occurs; "I might be like this" occurs; "I might be otherwise" occurs.
"There might be" occurs; "there might not be" occurs; "I might be thus" occurs;
"I might be in this way" occurs; "I might be otherwise" occurs.
And how does "I am" occur?
Without making any phenomenon non-occasional— whether it be form,
or feeling, or perception... [and so forth]...
Regarding volitional formations … [and so on] … regarding consciousness, one acquires the desire "I am," one acquires the conceit "I am," and one acquires the view "I am.
When that exists, these proliferations come to be.
"Or 'I am this,' or 'I am that,' or 'I am otherwise.
And how does the thought 'I am this' arise? One thinks:
'I am a khattiya,' or 'I am a brahmin,' or 'I am a vessa,' or 'I am a suddha,' or 'I am a householder.'"

Or: "I have gone forth," or "I am a god," or "I am a human," or "I possess form," or "I am formless," or "I possess perception," or "I am non-percipient," or "I am neither percipient nor non-percipient"—
thus there is the thought, "I am this."
And how does the thought "I am thus" arise?

By comparison with another person, thinking: "Just as he is a khattiya, so am I a khattiya," or "Just as he is a brahmin, so am I a brahmin," or "Just as he is a vessa, so am I a vessa," or "Just as he is a sudda, so am I..."
Or "I am pure"; or "Just as he is a householder, so am I a householder"; or "Just as he has gone forth, so have I gone forth";
or "Just as he is a deity, so am I a deity"; or "Just as he is a human being, so am I a human being";
or "Just as he possesses form, so do I possess form"; or "Just as he is formless, so am I formless."

Or, "As he is percipient, so am I percipient," or "As he is non-percipient, so am I non-percipient," or "As he is neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient, so am I neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient"—
thus there arises the thought, "I am exactly like this."
And how does the thought "I am otherwise" arise?

By comparison with another person, thinking: "As he is a khattiya, I am not such a khattiya," or "As he is a brahmin, I am not such a brahmin," or "As he is a vessa, I am not such a vessa," or as he is...
Just as he is a *sudda*, I am not a *sudda*; or just as he is a householder, I am not a householder;
or just as he has gone forth, I have not gone forth; or just as he is a deity, I am not a deity;
or just as he is a human, I am not a human; or just as he possesses form, I do not possess form.
or, "As he is formless, so am I formless"; or, "As he has perception, so do I have perception";
or, "As he is non-percipient, so am I non-percipient"; or, "As he is neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient, so am I neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient."
Thus, "I am otherwise" occurs.
And how does "I shall be" occur?
Without setting aside any phenomenon whatsoever, [one conceives] form... [and so on].
Feeling … perception … volitional formations … [and so on] … consciousness.

Regarding consciousness, one acquires desire for its future existence, one acquires conceit for its future existence, and one acquires views regarding its future existence. When that exists, these proliferations arise:
"It will be thus," or "It will be so," or "It will be otherwise."
And how does there come to be "I shall be thus"? [One thinks:
"I shall be a khattiya, or I shall be a brahmin, or I shall be a vessa, or I shall be a suddha;
or I shall be a householder, or I shall be one who has gone forth, or I shall be a deva, or a human being."
‘They will exist,’ or ‘they will be material,’ or ‘they will be immaterial,’ or ‘they will have perception,’ or ‘they will be non-percipient,’ or ‘they will be neither percipient nor non-percipient’—
thus there occurs the thought, ‘they will be such-and-such.’
And how does there come to be the thought, "I shall become thus"?
It is by comparing oneself with another person, thinking: "Just as he is a khattiya, so shall I become a khattiya," or "Just as he is a brahmin, so shall I become a brahmin" ... [and so on] ...
or "Just as he is one who is neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient, so shall I become one who is neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient."
"Thus it will be" is one way.
And how is there "it will be otherwise"?

By comparison with another person: "As he is a khattiya, I am not such a khattiya, but I shall become a khattiya," or, "As he is a brahmin, I am not such a brahmin, but I shall become a brahmin," and so forth.

Just as he is neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient, thinking "I shall not be neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient," or "I shall be neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient," or "I shall be otherwise than this"—
thus there is the thought "I am eternal.
And how does the thought "I am eternal" arise?
Having made some phenomenon non-secure, one thinks of form...
feeling... perception... volitional formations... or consciousness thus: "I am permanent, I am stable, I am eternal, I am subject to no change"—in this way, there is the thought "I am."
And how does one have the thought, "I am at peace"?
Without making any phenomenon an object of concern, one thinks:
"Form... feeling... perception... volitional formations... consciousness will be cut off, will perish; I shall not be."
Thus, there is the thought, "I am.
And how is there the thought, "May I be"?
Without setting aside any phenomenon whatsoever, [one regards] form... [and so on].
One acquires the desire that feeling... perception... volitional formations... consciousness might be; one acquires the conceit that they might be; one acquires the view that they might be.
When these exist, these proliferations arise:
"It might be thus," or "It might be so," or "It might be otherwise."
And how does the thought "May I be thus" arise?

[It arises as] "May I be a khattiya," or "May I be a brahmin," or "May I be a vessa," or "May I be a sudra," or "May I be a householder," or "May I be one gone forth," or "May I be a deva," or "May I be a human," or "May I be possessed of form."
Or, "May I be formless," or "May I have perception," or "May I be non-percipient," or "May I be neither percipient nor non-percipient"—
thus there comes to be the thought, "May I be such-and-such. And how does there come to be the thought, "May I be such-and-such"?
Comparing oneself with another person, thinking, "Just as he is a khattiya, may I too be a khattiya," or "Just as he is a brahmin, may I too be a brahmin," and so on, up to:
"Just as he is one who is neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient, may I too be one who is neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient"—
in this way there arises the thought, "May it be so."
And how does the thought "How might I be otherwise" arise?
It is by comparing oneself with another person, thinking: "As he is a khattiya, may I not be a khattiya like him," or "As he is a brahmin, may I not be a brahmin like him," and so on, up to:
"As he possesses the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, may I not possess the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception like him."
Thus there arises the thought, "It might be otherwise.
And how does the thought, "How might I not be? arise?
By making no allowance for any phenomenon whatsoever—whether form, or [any other aggregate]...
Feeling … perception … mental formations … [and so on] … consciousness.
One acquires the desire, "May I not be consciousness"; one acquires the conceit, "May I not be"; one acquires the view, "May I not be.
When that exists, these proliferations arise: "May I be this," or "May I be thus," or "May I be otherwise."
And how does the thought "May I be thus" arise? It arises as:
"May I be a khattiya," or "May I be a brāhmaṇa," or "May I be a vessa," or "May I be a sudda," or "May I be a householder," or "May I be one who has gone forth."

"May I not be a god," or "may I not be a human," or "may I not be possessed of form," or "may I not be formless," or "may I not be percipient," or "may I not be non-percipient," or "may I not be neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient"—
thus there arises the thought, "May I not be such-and-such."
And how does the thought "May I be thus" arise?
By comparison with another person, thinking: "Just as that khattiya is, may I be a khattiya," or "Just as that brahmin is, may I be a brahmin," and so on, up to:
"Just as that one who is neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient is, may I be one who is neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient."
Thus there arises the thought: "May I not be thus; may I be otherwise. And how does the thought "May I not be thus; may I be otherwise" arise?
By comparison with another person, thinking: "As that khattiya is, may I not be a khattiya like him," or "As that brahmin is, may I not be a brahmin like him," and so forth.
Thinking, "Just as he is neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient, may I not be like that neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient," or "May I be otherwise than this"—
thus there arises the thought, "May I be otherwise.
These eighteen modes of craving's wandering are based upon the internal.
In this regard, what are the eighteen modes of craving’s wandering based on the external?
There is: "By means of this, I am"; "By means of this, I am such"; "By means of this, I am exactly thus";
"By means of this, I am otherwise"; "By means of this, I shall be"; "By means of this, I shall be such"; "By means of this, I shall be exactly thus."
By this there is "I shall be"; by this there is "I shall be otherwise"; by this there is "I am"; by this there is "I am such";
by this there is "I might be"; by this there is "I might be thus"; by this there is "I might be so"; by this there is "I might be otherwise";
by this there is "I might not be"; by this there is "I might not be thus. By this...
"I might not be thus" occurs; "I might be otherwise than this" occurs.
And how does the thought "I am by means of this" occur?
Having made some phenomenon a basis, [one thinks] "form... and so forth.
Feeling … perception … mental formations … [and so on] … consciousness.
Through this consciousness, one acquires the desire "I am by means of this," one acquires the conceit "I am by means of this," and one acquires the view "I am by means of this.
When that exists, these proliferations arise:
"I am thus by means of this," or "I am exactly so by means of this," or "I am otherwise by means of this."
And how does one think "I am this" by means of this? One thinks:

"By means of this, I am a khattiya," or "by means of this, I am a brahmin," or "by means of this, I am a vessa," or "by means of this, I am a sudda," or "by means of this, I am a householder," or "by means of this, I am a renunciant," or "by means of this, I am a deva," or "by means of this, I am a human."
Or, by means of this [form], "I am material," or "I am immaterial," or "I am percipient," or "I am non-percipient," or "I am neither percipient nor non-percipient"—
thus, by means of this, there is the thought "I am such-and-such."
And how does the thought "I am equal to this" arise?
By comparing oneself with another person, thinking: "Just as he is a khattiya, so am I a khattiya," or "Just as he is a brahmin, so am I a brahmin," and so on, up to:
"Just as he possesses neither-perception-nor-non-perception, so do I possess neither-perception-nor-non-perception."
Thus, by means of this, there arises the thought:
"I am the same. And how, by means of this, does the thought "I am otherwise" arise?
By comparison with another person—such as, "As that kṣatriya is, I am not like that; I am a kṣatriya," or "As that brāhmaṇa is, I am not like that; I am a brāhmaṇa," and so forth...
Just as he is neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient, he does not think, "I am neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient because of this," nor does he think,
"In this way, I am otherwise because of this.
And how does the thought "I will be because of this" arise?
Having made some phenomenon an object, [one contemplates] form … feeling … perception …

Regarding volitional formations … regarding consciousness, one acquires desire for it thinking, “By means of this, there will be [existence]”; one acquires conceit for it thinking, “By means of this, there will be [existence]”;
one acquires views for it thinking, “By means of this, there will be [existence]. When that exists, these proliferations come to be.
"By this they will become thus; by this they will become so; by this they will become otherwise.
And how is it that "by this they will become thus"?

By this they will become khattiyas... [and so on] ...by this they will become formless, by this they will become percipient, by this they will become non-percipient, or by this they will become neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient.
Thus, by means of this, there comes to be "I shall become such-and-such.
And how does there come to be "I shall become thus" by means of this?
By comparing oneself with another person: "Just as that khattiya is, so shall I become a khattiya," or "Just as that brahmin is, so shall I become a brahmin," and so forth.
Just as he thinks, "As he is neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient, so shall I become neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient by means of this," thus there is the thought,
"By means of this, it will be thus. And how is there the thought,
"By means of this, it will be otherwise"?
Comparing oneself with another person, thinking: "As that kṣatriya is, I shall not be a kṣatriya in such a way," or "As that brahmin is, I shall not be a brahmin in such a way," and so on...

up to: "As he is one who is neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient, I shall not be one who is neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient in such a way"—thus there is the thought, "I shall become otherwise than this."
And how does the thought "I am not this" arise by means of this [contemplation]?
Having treated some phenomenon as something alien, one regards form...
feeling... [and so on].
Perception...
[and so on] ...volitional formations...
[and so on] ...consciousness: "By this I am permanent, I am stable, I am eternal, I am subject to the nature of non-change."
Thus, by this [method], there is the thought "I am this.
And how, by this [method], does the thought "I am that" arise?
Having made some phenomenon the object, [one regards] form... [and so on].
“Feeling… perception… volitional formations… consciousness will be cut off by this, will perish by this,
I will not exist by this”— thus, through this, there is the thought, “I am at ease. And how is it that through this there is the thought, “May I be”?
Having made some phenomenon an object,
[one contemplates] form … feeling … perception … [and so on].
Regarding volitional formations … pe … consciousness,

one acquires desire through the thought "may it be by means of this," one acquires conceit through the thought "may it be by means of this," and one acquires views through the thought "may it be by means of this. When that exists, these proliferations come to be.
"By this, it might be thus," or "by this, it might be so," or "by this, it might be otherwise.
And how is it that "by this, it might be thus"?
By this, one might be a khattiya; by this, one might be a brāhmaṇa; by this, one might be a vessa; by this...
"By this one may be a *sudda*, or by this one may be a householder, or by this one may be a renunciant, or by this one may be a deva, or by this one may be a human,
or by this one may be possessed of form, or by this one may be formless, or by this one may be percipient,
or by this one may be non-percipient, or by this one may be neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient."
Thus, by means of this, there arises the thought, "May it be thus.
And how does there arise the thought, "By means of this, may it be thus"?

By comparing oneself with another person, thinking: "Just as that khattiya is, may I too be a khattiya by means of this," or "Just as that brahmin is, may I too be a brahmin by means of this," and so forth...
Just as that one is neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient, thinking, "In this way may I be neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient through this," thus there is the thought, "May it be so through this.
And how is there the thought, "May it be otherwise through this"?
Comparing oneself with another person, thinking, "Just as he is a khattiya, may I not be a khattiya like him," or "Just as he is a brahmin, may I not be a brahmin like him," and so on...
up to "Just as he is one who is neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient, may I not be one who is neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient like him"—
this is "being otherwise than this."
And how does the thought "May I not be through this" arise?
Having treated some phenomenon as disagreeable, [one thinks] of form...
feeling... [and so on].

One acquires desire for perception... for volitional formations... for consciousness, thinking, "May I be by means of this"; one acquires conceit, thinking, "May I be by means of this"; one acquires views, thinking, "May I be by means of this."
When that exists, these proliferations arise:
"By means of this, may I be such," or "By means of this, may I be thus," or "By means of this, may I be otherwise.
And how does the thought "By means of this, may I be such" occur?

"By this means may I become a khattiya," or "by this means may I become a brāhmaṇa," or "by this means may I become a vessa," or "by this means may I become a sudda," or "by this means may I become a householder," or "by this means may I become a renunciant," or "by this means may I become a deva," or "by this means may I become a human."

"By means of this, may I be thus: 'May I be material by means of this,' or 'May I be immaterial by means of this,' or 'May I be percipient by means of this,' or 'May I be non-percipient by means of this,' or 'May I be neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient by means of this'—thus there arises the thought: 'By means of this, may I be such-and-such.'"
And how does the thought "By this means, may I become thus" arise?
It is by comparing oneself with another person, thinking: "Just as that khattiya is, may I by this means become a khattiya"; or "Just as that brahmin is, may I by this means become a brahmin"...
[and so on] ...or "Just as that one who is neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient is, may I by this means become one who is neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient."
Thus, there arises the thought: "In this way, by means of this, may I become thus.
And how does the thought arise: "In this way, by means of this, may I become otherwise"?
By comparing oneself with another person, one thinks: "Just as that kṣatriya is, may I not be a kṣatriya in this way," or, "Just as that brahmin is, may I not be a brahmin in this way," and so forth.
Thinking, "Just as he is neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient, may I not be like that neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient," or "May I be otherwise than he is"—
this is how there comes to be the thought, "May I be different from him.
These eighteen modes of craving's roaming are based on external things.
Thus, these eighteen modes of craving’s movement are based on the internal, and these eighteen modes of craving’s movement are based on the external;
having combined and condensed them together, there are thirty-six modes of craving’s movement.
Thus, there are thirty-six such past modes of craving’s movement and thirty-six future modes of craving’s movement.
The thirty-six modes of craving’s wandering in the present: having gathered these together and condensed them into one, there are one hundred and eight modes of craving’s wandering.
In that regard, what are the sixty-two positions on views as spoken by the Blessed One in the *Brahmajāla* exposition?
There are four eternalists, four partial-eternalists, four who hold to the finite-and-infinite views, four who resort to evasive wrangling,

two who maintain the doctrine of fortuitous origination, sixteen who maintain the doctrine of percipient immortality, eight who maintain the doctrine of non-percipient immortality, eight who maintain the doctrine of neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient immortality,
seven annihilationists, and five who maintain the doctrine of Nibbāna in the present life.
"These sixty-two positions of view were spoken by the Blessed One in the Brahmajāla Sutta.
The Analysis of the Minor Subjects (Khuddakavatthuvibhaṅga) is finished.
